 I keep seeing “power outage” everywhere online. I scroll through my Instagram and see checklists of what to buy. My TikTok is filled with people trying to make commissions selling battery-powered torches. But let’s be realistic: we can't all afford to buy a full power-outage kit outright.
 Nor do most of us have a place to store it. And while I really do want to be prepared, I’m not going to head to my local grocery store with a list of 50 items — that’d be my entire weekly food budget in one shop.
 Instead, I’ve whittled it down to the 9 items you’d really need if a blackout lasts longer than an hour or two. You may already own some of these items, but if they’re tucked away, it might be smart to put them together, perhaps in a bag or box, ready to grab when needed.

Each one stores power in a lithium iron phosphate battery, runs silently indoors, and refills from a wall outlet or a solar panel, which is why they have become the first thing coastal homeowners buy.
 I have been putting these stations through real household loads for the past two months: a refrigerator nursing through compressor cycles, a CPAP machine running overnight, a router and a laptop, and a window unit where the household could stand it. What surprised me most was not the peak output figures. It was how much the honest runtime math mattered.
 Marketing calls these machines solar generators, but they are battery power stations. Panels are almost never included unless the box says so, and during a hurricane the panels are the one part you cannot rely on.  Smallest budget kit: DaranEner 288Wh with a bundled 40W panel and a 4-mode LED light.

 How We Chose These 12 Solar Generators
 We ranked these on published specifications, owner review patterns and our own load testing, and we did not buy into headline runtime claims without checking them.
 Every station in this guide was run against a real refrigerator cycling overnight, a sustained 450W window air conditioner where output allowed it, and a mixed load of router, laptop, lights and phone charging. We logged wall-clock runtime and checked it against the arithmetic in the sizing section below.
 We also weighed warranty length, battery cycle rating, recharge speed from a wall outlet before a storm, idle self-consumption, and whether capacity can grow later. Where owner reviews repeatedly flag a limit, we say so rather than burying it.
 Two honest caveats. We did not test solar recharge inside storm conditions, because no lab safely simulates hurricane cloud cover. And several of these stations include a companion app, and app-only controls are a real inconvenience when your phone battery is one of the things you are rationing.
 What Size Solar Generator Do You Actually Need for a Hurricane?
 Start here: runtime equals usable watt-hours multiplied by 0.85, divided by your load in watts. The 0.85 factor accounts for inverter conversion loss and the battery management system holding a reserve. Nothing else matters until you have that number.
 Build your load list first. A refrigerator compressor averages roughly 150W once it is cycling, but it draws around 700W at startup. LED lighting runs 10W per room, a router about 15W, a laptop 60W, phone charging 10-20W, and a CPAP machine sits near 40W. Add those up as running watts, then check that your station’s surge rating clears the biggest single startup draw on the list.
 Now work the formula against a 270W blended essential load, which is roughly a refrigerator, three rooms of lights and device charging:
 288Wh station: 288 x 0.85 / 270 = about 0.9 hours
 1024Wh station: 1024 x 0.85 / 270 = about 3.2 hours
 1152Wh station: 1152 x 0.85 / 270 = about 3.6 hours
 2010Wh station: 2010 x 0.85 / 270 = about 6.3 hours
 2073.6Wh station: 2073.6 x 0.85 / 270 = about 6.5 hours
 3072Wh station: 3072 x 0.85 / 270 = about 9.7 hours
 3584Wh station: 3584 x 0.85 / 270 = about 11.3 hours
 3600Wh station: 3600 x 0.85 / 270 = about 11.3 hours
 4096Wh station: 4096 x 0.85 / 270 = about 12.9 hours
 That is one evening of essential power, not a week. Gulf and Atlantic outages commonly run three to seven days, and anyone planning to run a refrigerator without rationing needs a station in the 3,500Wh class or paired with a generator.
 Against a single 450W window air conditioner, the arithmetic is harsher: a 2073.6Wh station gives about 3.9 hours, a 3584Wh station about 6.8 hours, and a 4096Wh station about 7.7 hours. Against a 700W compressor load, even the 4096Wh station drops to under five hours.
 If a medical device is involved, size it separately. A CPAP machine at 40W for eight hours draws about 320Wh, so a 1024Wh station covers three nights. An oxygen concentrator draws several hundred watts continuously and pushes most 1kWh stations toward their limit on the first night.

 What to Look for in a Hurricane-Ready Solar Generator
 Capacity in watt-hours is the headline, but inverter efficiency, idle draw and chemistry decide how that capacity performs in practice. A 2000Wh station with 20W of overhead gives you less usable energy than a 2000Wh station drawing 6W, and the difference shows up on night three of an outage.
 Check continuous output against your largest running load, and check surge against your largest startup load. Refrigerator compressors routinely draw several times their rated running watts when they kick in, and a unit that browns out every time the fridge cycles will not nurse food through a week.
 Battery chemistry matters more than most shoppers expect. Every station in this roundup uses lithium iron phosphate rather than the older lithium-ion NMC chemistry, which is the right call for emergency equipment. The cycle ratings here range from about 3,000 to 10,000 cycles, and all of them tolerate being left partly charged far better than NMC packs.
 Look at UPS switchover time if you have computers, network gear, or medical equipment. Anything under 20ms is treated as seamless; the EcoFlow models and the Anker SOLIX S2000 sit in that range.
 Solar input wattage tells you how fast the unit can rebuild in bad weather, but check whether the input voltage ceiling matches the panels you can realistically deploy. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 caps solar input at 60V, and the EcoFlow DELTA Pro limits its single port to 15A, which is a real ceiling on array size.
 Expandability is the single biggest factor for anyone planning for a long outage. Stations that cannot add a battery have a hard ceiling, and the ones that reach 12.3kWh, 21kWh or 25kWh give you room to change your mind later.
 Finally, count the outlets against your household, and weigh the unit against your evacuation plan. Anything above 80 lb realistically stays where it is, and anything above 100 lb belongs in a garage or utility room rather than a hallway.
 Solar Generator vs Gas Generator for Hurricane Season
 A battery station wins on safety and fuel independence. A gas generator wins on runtime and heavy loads. For most coastal households the honest answer is that both belong in the plan, used at different hours.
 Gas generators produce carbon monoxide, which is fatal at concentrations that are easy to reach in a closed house. The Consumer Product Safety Commission has documented more than a hundred portable generator deaths a year in the United States, and the safety guidance is to run them outdoors at least 20 feet from any opening. That rule alone disqualifies them for apartments, condos, HOAs and any home where you cannot guarantee 20 feet of clearance.
 Solar generators have no fuel, no exhaust and no moving parts. They run between 25dB and 30dB, so you can sleep next to one. They need no fuel deliveries that may become impossible after a storm, and the fuel queue problem that hits gas stations in the first 48 hours simply does not apply.
 The downsides of a battery station are equally clear. Storage is finite and purchases are expensive per watt-hour, output is limited compared with any fuel generator, and recharging depends on grid power, a solar panel or a gas generator. A station with 3000Wh that wants a 450W air conditioner will not last the night.
 For a long outage, the hybrid rhythm wins. Run the gas engine outdoors during daylight hours to recharge the battery or, better, run the loads directly, then shut it down at night and use battery power indoors where it is quiet and safe. Several of the stations here, including the DELTA Pro, the DELTA Pro 3 and the HomePower 3600 Plus, accept generator charging specifically for this pattern.
 Prepper forums tend to land in the same place: gas for heavy loads, battery for overnight quiet. We think that is right, and it is why the Anker SOLIX C300 and the DaranEner kit earn a place in a roundup that mostly covers 1000Wh-plus machines.
 Solar Panel Sizing and Post-Storm Recharge Math
 Size panels with a derate, not a nameplate. Multiply array watts by roughly 0.75 for real-world conversion losses, then by usable peak sun hours for your location and season, and that is your realistic daily harvest.
 Worked example: a 200W panel at 0.75 derate with 5 peak sun hours produces roughly 750Wh in a day. Against a 270W essential load that is about 2.8 hours of runtime recovered. A 400W array produces about 1500Wh, and a 1000W array produces about 3750Wh, which covers a full day of 270W use with margin.
 Now apply the post-storm haircut. Heavy cloud after a hurricane can cut output to a third of expected, so a 750Wh daily harvest might realistically become 250Wh. Plan for panels to slow the drain, not to reverse it.
 The 20 rule is a useful heuristic for people asking how many panels they need: your daily consumption in watt-hours, divided by 5 peak sun hours with a 0.75 derate, gives you the array size in watts. For a 3000Wh daily need, that works out to roughly 800W of panels, and most units here will need two ports or a higher-voltage input to accept that.
 Bring panels in before the eyewall arrives. Portable folding panels are not rated for hurricane wind or debris, and a panel that goes airborne damages homes and drains your battery budget at the worst possible time.

 Hurricane Prep Checklist
 Before the season, charge every station to full from the wall, confirm the included cables fit, and run one full discharge test on your essential load list. Write the runtime number down next to each appliance so you are not doing arithmetic in a dark house.
 Before the season, update each app and firmware version, and set a monthly calendar reminder to top the battery up to around 80% between storms. Lithium iron phosphate cells self-discharge slowly, and storing at a mid-level charge is kinder to long-term capacity than sitting full for months.
 Before the season, test your actual 240V loads if you have them. Switch on a well pump or pump motor and confirm the station holds steady through startup, which is the single most common surprise for new buyers.
 When a watch is issued, top every station to full and disable any scheduled charge limits. Move the units to their planned indoor positions, because moving a 99 lb station in a flooded or dark house is a poor use of storm hours.
 When a watch is issued, set up your solar array away from windows and away from the reach of wind-driven debris, but be ready to bring it in before the strongest bands arrive. Charge the station during daylight before the worst conditions, since cloud cover will cut output during the storm itself.
 During the outage, run a load budget rather than running everything. A refrigerator, a CPAP or oxygen machine, two LED lamps, the router and phone charging is a defensible core. Anything beyond that should be switched off until you have recharged.
 During the outage, keep food safe by keeping the fridge closed. FoodSafety.gov guidance treats an unopened refrigerator as safe for about four hours and a full freezer for roughly 48 hours, so a thermometer in the fridge is worth more than any battery calculation.
 After the storm, recharge from the wall first if grid power is back, then run the solar array during daylight hours. Do not leave a station at zero for a week expecting to bring it back, since deeply discharged lithium packs can take a long time to recover and some management systems will refuse to charge.

 For 240V loads and whole-home ambitions, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is the only station here that handles split-phase output and expands past 12kWh. For apartments and rentals where a combustion engine is not an option, the Anker SOLIX C300 is the one I would carry up the stairs.
 None of this replaces a generator for a week of cooking, air conditioning and water heating. The best hurricane plan pairs a battery station for overnight medical devices, refrigeration and communications with a gas engine run outdoors during daylight hours, recharging the battery between uses.
 Whichever you choose, run a full discharge test before the season and write your runtime numbers down. Our home backup guide goes deeper on sizing for fixed installations, and 2026 is a good year to stop treating this as a weekend project.

 How many hours will each one run your essentials?
 We modeled a typical "keep the house functional" outage load: a refrigerator, Wi-Fi router and modem, LED lighting, a TV for a few hours and phone and laptop charging. That adds up to about 2.6 kWh per day . We then assumed 85% of the rated battery is usable after inverter losses, which matches independent measurements of current LFP power stations.
 The takeaway: a 2 kWh unit covers an overnight outage. For a 2-3 day storm outage without solar, you need 5 kWh or more, or a smaller unit plus panels to refill it every day.
 Price per kWh: what you actually pay for storage
 Inverter wattage gets the headlines, but battery capacity is what keeps the lights on. Dividing price by capacity is the fastest way to compare value.
 The cheapest storage per kWh is in the 2-3.6 kWh, 120V class. You pay a premium of roughly $150-200 per kWh for 240V output and higher-wattage inverters (HomePower 3600 Pro Max, the Mango Power E 240V kit, Apex 300). That premium is worth it only if you actually have 240V loads.
 How to choose: 5 questions before you buy
 1. Essentials or whole-home?
 Essentials backup (fridge, internet, lights, medical devices) needs 2-4 kWh and a 120V unit. Whole-home backup that includes a well pump, central air or an electric range needs 240V output, 6,000 W or more, and 10 kWh+ of expandable storage.
 2. Do you have 240V appliances?
 Most US well pumps, many sump pumps over 1 HP, central AC, electric dryers and ranges run on 240V. A 120V-only power station cannot start them. Of the seven picks, the HomePower 3600 Pro Max, the Mango Power E 240V kit and Apex 300 support 240V.
 3. What will start, not just what will run?

 Solar is what turns a battery into a multi-day backup system. A rough rule: daily solar harvest ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.8 . For example, 800 W of panels × 5 sun hours × 0.8 ≈ 3.2 kWh per day, enough to refill a 3.5 kWh unit on a clear day.  For essentials, you can plug appliances straight into the unit. To power hardwired circuits, you need a transfer switch, a home power panel or a power inlet with an interlock, installed by a licensed electrician. Never backfeed a home through a dryer outlet.  Frequently asked questions
 What size solar generator do I need for home backup?
 For essentials (fridge, internet, lights, phone charging), plan on 2-4 kWh of battery and 2,500-3,600 W of output. For a well pump or other 240V loads, choose a 120/240V unit with 4,000 W or more, such as the Mango Power E 240V kit (6,000 W) or the Jackery HomePower 3600 Pro Max (4,000 W at 240V).
 Can a solar generator run a whole house?
 Yes, if it has 240V split-phase output, enough capacity and a proper connection to your panel. Expect 10-20 kWh of expandable storage, a transfer switch or home power panel, and a solar array to recharge daily. Central AC and electric heat are usually the loads people choose to leave off.
 How long will a solar generator run a refrigerator?
 A modern fridge uses about 1.2-1.8 kWh per day. A 2 kWh unit runs it alone for roughly 1 day, a 3.6 kWh unit for about 2 days and a 5 kWh unit for about 3 days, before solar recharging.
 Do I need 240V output?
 Only if you need to run 240V appliances during an outage: well pumps, central AC, electric dryers, ranges or some large sump pumps. If your must-run list is the fridge, internet, lights and medical devices, 120V is enough and costs less per kWh.
 How many solar panels do I need to recharge a solar generator?
 Multiply panel watts by your peak sun hours and by 0.8 for losses. 800 W of panels in 5 sun hours produces about 3.2 kWh per day, which refills a 3-3.5 kWh battery on a sunny day.
 Is there still a federal tax credit for solar generators?
 The 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit (25D) does not apply to expenditures made after December 31, 2025. Some states and utilities still offer battery storage incentives, so check locally.

 Highlights
 TL;DR: A solar generator is a portable power station paired with solar panels, so it makes its own power instead of just storing it. Our top picks: the Jackery Solar Generator 2000 Plus Kit (best overall), the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Solar Kit (best for whole-home backup), the BLUETTI AC200L + SP200L Kit (best value), the BLUETTI AC180 solar kit (best budget), and the Jackery Solar Generator 1000 v2 (best for camping). The spec that matters most: solar input watts, not just battery capacity.
 Power outages aren’t getting shorter. The average U.S. customer lost about  11 hours to power interruptions in 2024 , the U.S. Energy Information Administration reports, nearly double the yearly average from the decade before.
 A gas generator can bridge that gap. So can a solar generator, minus the fumes, the noise, and the trips to the gas station.
 But “solar generator” gets thrown around loosely. Plenty of listings use the term for a battery that’s never seen a solar panel. We only recommend kits here that actually pair a power station with real solar input, and we picked them based on how fast they recharge from the sun, not just how big the battery is.

 What Is a Solar Generator, Exactly?
 A solar generator is a portable power station connected to one or more solar panels, so the battery recharges from sunlight instead of only a wall outlet.  EcoFlow’s own breakdown of the two categories  puts it simply: a power station stores energy, a solar generator actively makes it.
 That distinction matters more than marketing copy suggests. A power station without panels is just a big rechargeable battery. It’ll get you through an outage once, then it’s dead until you find an outlet.
 Add solar panels and the equation changes. As long as the sun’s out, you’re topping the battery back up. That’s the real value of a solar generator over a  gas generator : you’re not driving anywhere for fuel.
 Jackery’s guide to the difference between a solar generator, a power station, and a solar panel  makes the same point: if you buy a power station and solar panels separately, you’ve built a solar generator setup yourself. Buying a kit just bundles the two so you don’t have to match specs on your own.
 What Size Solar Generator Do You Need?
 Match the battery to what you actually plan to run, not the biggest number you can afford. A 1,000 to 2,000Wh battery covers phones, a router, some lights, and a mini fridge through a short outage. Anything bigger, especially a full-size fridge or a window AC unit, needs 2,000Wh or more.
 Two numbers decide what a solar generator can do for you: watt-hours (Wh) and watts (W). Watt-hours are the fuel tank, they tell you how long the battery lasts. Watts are the engine, they tell you what you can plug in at once without tripping the inverter.
 Running a full-size fridge at roughly 150W alongside internet and a few lights drains a 2,000Wh battery in about 10 to 20 hours. If you want to see exactly what your gear would pull from one of these, our breakdown of  what a portable power station can actually run  walks through real appliance math.
 Best Solar Generators of 2026
 These five kits cover the range from weekend camping to keeping the lights on through a multi-day outage. All of them ship with, or offer, real solar panels rated for meaningful input wattage, not a token 30W trickle charger.
 1. Jackery Solar Generator 2000 Plus Kit (Best Overall) 
 This kit pairs the Explorer 2000 Plus with two SolarSaga 200W panels. The battery starts at 2,042Wh and expands to 12kWh with add-on packs, which is enough headroom to grow from “backup for a few rooms” to “backup for most of the house” without replacing the unit. It handles up to 6,000W of combined output in parallel setups and takes solar input up to 400W across the two panels.

 2. EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 Solar Kit (Best for Whole-Home Backup) 
 The  DELTA Pro 3 so l ar kit  is built for people who want a real alternative to a whole-home generator. It holds 4,096Wh out of the box, expands to 48kWh, and outputs 4,000W (6,000W with X-Boost). Its solar input tops out at 2,600W across two MPPT ports, with 99% tracking efficiency, so it recharges faster from the sun than most home-backup units on the market.

 The  AC200L solar kit  lands in the middle of the pack on price for what it delivers: 2,048Wh of storage, 2,400W of output, and up to 1,200W of solar input. That input number is the story here. It’ll pull a full recharge from the sun in a fraction of the time a similarly sized unit with a 200W or 300W solar cap would need. It also expands to 8,192Wh if you outgrow the base unit.

 For readers who want real solar charging without the flagship price tag, the  AC180  pairs a 1,152Wh battery with up to 500W of solar input, which is generous for this size class. Add a 200W panel and you’re looking at a recharge window well under 10 hours in decent sun, according to BLUETTI’s own charging figures.

 The  Solar Generator 1000 v2 kit  is built around Jackery’s smaller Explorer 1000 v2, which weighs under 24 pounds and hits a 1-hour fast charge from AC power. It still takes up to 400W of solar input, so a couple of hours of good sun gets you most of the way back to full. If your use case leans more toward  camping trips than outages , this is the pick to start with.

 How Fast Do Solar Panels Actually Recharge These?
 Charging time from solar comes down to three things: panel wattage, hours of direct sun, and how efficient the built-in charge controller is. Most solar generators worth buying use MPPT (maximum power point tracking) controllers, which  pull up to 25% more usable power from the same panels than older PWM controllers .
 As a rough rule of thumb, aim for solar wattage that can refill your battery in 5 to 6 hours of peak sun. A 2,000Wh battery pairs well with 400 to 500W of panels. Undersize the panels and you’ll be waiting two or three days for a full charge instead of one afternoon.
 Cloud cover, panel angle, and time of year all cut into that number too. Treat manufacturer charge-time estimates as a best case, not a guarantee.
 Solar Generator vs. Gas Generator for Outages
 A solar generator wins on convenience and safety for most home backup needs. It produces no carbon monoxide, so it’s safe to run indoors, and it’s quiet enough to sit next to while you sleep. A gas generator needs to run outdoors, needs fuel you have to store and rotate, and needs maintenance to start reliably when you actually need it.
 Where gas still wins: raw output for whole-house loads like central air, and the ability to refuel instantly at 2 a.m. instead of waiting for daylight. If you’re weighing the two head to head, our full  solar generator vs. gas generator comparison breaks down the tradeoffs in more detail.
 For camping specifically, the calculus tilts even further toward solar. No fuel to haul, no fumes near the tent, and panels that do double duty charging phones and running a cooler during the day.
 Do You Need the Home Backup Size or the Portable Size?
 If your goal is keeping a fridge, router, and a few lights running through a multi-day outage, you want the 2,000Wh-plus tier, closer to the DELTA Pro 3 or AC200L in this list. Our full  home backup power station picks  go deeper on sizing a system for that use case specifically.
 If you mainly need something for weekend trips, tailgating, or a laptop and phone during a shorter outage, the smaller kits like the Jackery 1000 v2 or the AC180 make more sense. Don’t pay for capacity you won’t use. If budget is the deciding factor over sizing, our  power stations under $500  roundup covers the entry-level tier without solar bundled in, useful if you want to add panels separately later.
 Is a Solar Generator Worth It?
 For most homeowners in outage-prone areas, yes. The upfront cost is higher than a comparable gas generator, but there’s no ongoing fuel cost, no annual maintenance visit, and no carbon monoxide risk. Over a few years of outages, that gap narrows fast.
 The honest caveat: a solar generator won’t run central air or a well pump for days on end the way a whole-home gas or propane system can. It’s built for the “keep the essentials running comfortably” tier of backup, not total energy independence. For most households, that’s exactly the gap that needs filling.
 If you’re deciding between EcoFlow, Jackery, and BLUETTI specifically, our  EcoFlow vs. Jackery vs. BLUETTI comparison  breaks down how the three brands differ beyond just this list.
 Pick the size that matches what you actually need to run, check that the solar input watts match your panel setup, and you’ll have a system that earns its keep the next time the grid goes down.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a solar generator power a whole house? 
 A large unit like the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 , especially when expanded with extra battery packs, can cover most essential circuits during an outage. It won’t run everything at once the way a whole-home standby generator does, but it can keep a fridge, lights, internet, and small appliances running for days.
 How long do solar generators last? 
 Most current models use LiFePO4 batteries, which are rated for thousands of charge cycles, often 3,000 to 4,500 depending on the brand, before capacity drops meaningfully. Used a few times a year for backup, that translates to well over a decade of useful life.
 Do I need special solar panels, or will any panel work? 
 You need a panel that matches your unit’s voltage and connector type, or you’ll need an adapter. Manufacturer-matched panels (Jackery SolarSaga, EcoFlow’s own panels, BLUETTI’s PV series) are the safest bet since they’re tuned for that unit’s MPPT controller and won’t need extra troubleshooting.
 Is a solar generator worth it over a gas generator? 
 For most homeowners dealing with occasional outages, yes. You skip the fuel storage, the noise, and the carbon monoxide risk, and you can run it indoors. Gas still wins if you need to power heavy whole-house loads like central air for extended periods.
 Can a solar generator charge on a cloudy day? 
 Yes, but slower. Solar panels still produce power in overcast conditions, typically 10 to 25% of their rated output, so a charge that takes 5 hours in full sun might take most of a day under heavy cloud cover.
